passages.happening:
The heading reads, “For the choirmaster. With stringed instruments. A Psalm of David” (verse 1).

The prayer opens with a plea and a memory: “Answer me when I call, O God of my righteousness! You have relieved my distress; show me grace and hear my prayer” (verse 1).

Then the man turns and speaks to the people who are attacking him. “How long, O men, will my honor be maligned? How long will you love vanity and seek after lies?” (verse 2). He tells them, “Know that the LORD has set apart the godly for Himself; the LORD hears when I call to Him” (verse 3).

Then he gives them, or himself, a counsel for the night: “Be angry, yet do not sin; on your bed, search your heart and be still” (verse 4). “Offer the sacrifices of the righteous and trust in the LORD” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
The heading shows that this psalm was used in public worship, most likely at the temple in Jerusalem. The choirmaster was the leader of the music. ‘Stringed instruments’ means harps and lyres.

‘God of my righteousness’ means the God who knows I am in the right, the God who will defend my cause.

‘Maligned’ means spoken against, slandered. ‘Vanity’ means what is empty, worth nothing. The man's enemies are spreading lies about him and loving what has no weight.

‘The godly’ in verse 3 is a Hebrew word built from hesed, God's loyal love. The godly are the people who belong to God and keep faith with him.

‘Sacrifices of the righteous’ means offerings brought to God's altar with a right heart, not as a way of bending God to one's will.

Verse 4 is hard to translate. The Hebrew verb means to be stirred up, to shake. It can be used of shaking with fear or of shaking with anger. So some Bibles read ‘tremble, and do not sin’: stand in awe of God and stop. The Greek Old Testament read it as anger, and the Berean Standard Bible does too: ‘Be angry, yet do not sin.’ Both readings end in the same quiet place: on your bed, search your heart, and be still.
passages.later:
Paul quotes verse 4 word for word as the Greek Old Testament gives it: “Be angry, yet do not sin.” Do not let the sun set upon your anger (Ephesians 4:26). He goes on: “and do not give the devil a foothold” (Ephesians 4:27). For Paul the verse does not forbid every anger. It forbids anger that is kept, fed and carried to bed unresolved.

The same letter also says, “Get rid of all bitterness, rage and anger” (Ephesians 4:31). James writes that people should be “slow to anger, for man's anger does not bring about the righteousness that God desires” (James 1:19-20).

Jesus himself was angry. Mark says he looked at those who opposed healing on the Sabbath “with anger and sorrow at their hardness of heart” (Mark 3:5).
passages.hard:
Is anger a sin? Read with Ephesians 4:26, this verse says anger itself is not always wrong. There is right anger at evil and injustice. Jesus was angry (Mark 3:5). But anger turns easily into sin: into hatred, revenge, cruel words or violence. So the psalm gives a practice, not a feeling: lie down, search your heart, be still.

Some readers prefer the reading ‘tremble’. On that reading the man is telling his enemies to tremble before God and stop sinning. That reading is fair to the Hebrew too. The Berean Standard Bible follows the Greek, as Paul did.

If anger has become something you cannot control, or if anger at home has made anyone afraid, that is more than a verse can fix. Please talk to someone you trust, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Do you take your anger to bed with you? The psalm suggests a different way to end a hard day: lie still, look honestly at your own heart, and trust God with what you cannot fix. Try it tonight before sleep.

passages.t: More joy than a full harvest, and sleep in peace
passages.happening:
The psalm turns to the worried crowd. “Many ask, ‘Who can show us the good?’” (verse 6). The man answers with a prayer: “Shine the light of Your face upon us, O LORD” (verse 6).

He tells God what God has done for him: “You have filled my heart with more joy than when grain and new wine abound” (verse 7).

And he ends the day: “I will lie down and sleep in peace, for You alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
‘Who can show us the good?’ sounds like people in hard times. Some readers think of a drought or a poor harvest, because verse 7 speaks of grain and wine. The psalm does not say what the trouble was.

‘The light of Your face’ comes from the blessing the priests spoke over Israel. In it the priests prayed that the LORD would make his face shine on his people (Numbers 6:25). A king's bright face meant he was pleased and kind: “When a king's face brightens, there is life” (Proverbs 16:15). For God's face to shine on you meant his favour and his peace.

Harvest was the happiest time of the farming year. A full harvest of grain, and of grapes pressed for new wine, meant food for the year ahead and a feast. The man says God has given him a joy greater than that.

Psalm 3 was a prayer on waking. Psalm 4 is a prayer for lying down. Many have prayed it as an evening prayer. ‘You alone’ is the point: not his guards, not his walls, not his harvest.
passages.later:
The priestly blessing behind verse 6 reads, “may the LORD cause His face to shine upon you and be gracious to you” (Numbers 6:25).

Habakkuk sings of the same kind of joy, deeper than harvest: even if “the fields produce no food”, he says, “yet I will exult in the LORD” (Habakkuk 3:17-18).

Proverbs promises the same rest: “When you lie down, you will not be afraid; when you rest, your sleep will be sweet” (Proverbs 3:24).

Paul tells the church in Philippi that God's peace, “which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 4:7).
passages.asks:
Ask where you look for ‘the good’: a full bank account, a full barn, good news. The psalm points to a joy that does not depend on the harvest.

Many people lie awake. If sleep will not come, you might pray verse 8 slowly, more than once. And if sleeplessness goes on for weeks, it is wise to see a doctor; that is not a failure of faith.
